questions.question: Calculate the four operating-cycle indicators for Molefe and de Waal Traders and interpret them together as one story.
questions.expected_answer: Stock turnover rate: cost of sales R1 640 000 over average stock of R190 000 — opening R194 800 and closing R185 200 — gives 8,6 times a year. Stock holding period: average stock over cost of sales times 365 gives 42,3 days per refill — the same fact as the rate, in days. Debtors' collection period: average debtors R54 000 over credit sales of R1 476 000, times 365, gives 13,4 days — excellent against 30-day terms. Creditors' payment period: average creditors R83 000 over credit purchases of R1 245 000, times 365, gives 24,3 days. Read together: money is locked in stock about 42 days and in debtors about 13 — roughly 55 days from buying stock to banking cash — while suppliers are paid at day 24, so the gap is financed by the business's own money. Collections are superb; the six-week shelf suits a hardware trade but should be watched; and paying at 24 days on 30-day terms hands back about six days of free credit unless an early-settlement discount justifies it.

questions.question: Calculate the debt-equity ratio and the return on average partners' equity, and give a full comment on each, including the case for or against more borrowing.
questions.expected_answer: Debt-equity: non-current liabilities R138 000 to equity R765 800 gives 0,2 to 1 — for every rand of the partners' money, outsiders have twenty cents of long-term money. This is low gearing: safe, with little exposure to interest rates. But since the business earns far more on its funds than the loan's 12 percent cost, a case exists for gearing up carefully to expand — borrowing is worthwhile whenever the return on borrowed money exceeds its cost. Return on average partners' equity: net profit R421 000 over average equity R734 300 — opening R702 800 and closing R765 800 — gives 57,3 percent. Compared with roughly 8 to 10 percent risk-free in a fixed deposit, the return is outstanding; the comment must acknowledge that the partners' own labour sits inside the figure, since their salaries are appropriations and not expenses, yet even after mentally pricing that labour the investment comfortably beats the alternative. Solvency confirms safety: total assets to total liabilities is 4,3 to 1.

questions.question: Write a four-part comment on the liquidity of the business, and explain why an indicator must never be judged alone.
questions.expected_answer: Figure and comparison: the current ratio is 4,1 to 1 — current assets R375 550 to current liabilities R91 750 — and the acid-test is 2,1 to 1, both well above the traditional comfort levels of about 2 to 1 and 1 to 1. Direction: liquidity is very strong — short-term debts are covered even if no further stock is sold. Cause: fast debtor collections at 13,4 days and a large bank balance of over R130 000 keep liquid assets high. Consequence and advice: the business cannot be embarrassed by a payday, but it is over-liquid — idle cash earns almost nothing — so the partners should put surplus funds to work: expansion, reducing the 12 percent loan, or earning early-settlement discounts. Indicators must be read in pairs because one number can carry two stories: a rising current ratio can mean strengthening liquidity or unsold stock piling up, and only the stock holding period decides which; likewise a turnover rate rising and a holding period falling are the same news in two dialects. Every figure needs its comparison — last year, the norm, the policy — before it means anything.
